etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English way, wey, from Old English weġ, from Proto-West Germanic *weg, from Proto-Germanic *wegaz, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Doublet of voe and possibly via.

definitions.definition: A road, a direction, a (physical or conceptual) path from one place to another.

quote.text: The way seems difficult, and steep to scale.

quote.citation: 1688 November 15 (Gregorian calendar), John Evelyn, “[Diary entry for 5 November 1688]”, in William Bray, editor, Memoirs, Illustrative of the Life and Writings of John Evelyn, […], 2nd edition, volume I, London: Henry Colburn, […]; and sold by John and Arthur Arch, […], published 1819, →OCLC:
quote.text: the season and ways very improper for his Majesty's forces to march so great a distance

quote.text: Judge Short had gone to town, and Farrar was off for a three days' cruise up the lake. I was bitterly regretting I had not gone with him when the distant notes of a coach horn reached my ear, and I descried a four-in-hand winding its way up the inn road from the direction of Mohair.

quote.text: I was on my way to the door, but all at once, through the fog in my head, I began to sight one reef that I hadn't paid any attention to afore.

quote.text: Risk is everywhere. […] For each one there is a frighteningly precise measurement of just how likely it is to jump from the shadows and get you. “The Norm Chronicles” […] aims to help data-phobes find their way through this blizzard of risks.

definitions.definition: A means to enter or leave a place.

quote.text: Just under the ceiling there were three lunette windows, heavily barred and blacked out in the normal way by centuries of grime. Their bases were on a level with the pavement outside, a narrow way which was several feet lower than the road behind the house.

definitions.definition: A roughly-defined geographical area.
(heading) To do with a place or places.
(with 'the', usually with modifier) A set of values and customs associated with and seen as central to the identity of a group of people.
A method or manner of doing something; a mannerism.

quote.text: “[…] That woman is stark mad, Lord Stranleigh. […] If she had her way, she’d ruin the company inside a year with her hare-brained schemes ; love of the people, and that sort of guff.”

quote.text: She was a fat, round little woman, richly apparelled in velvet and lace,  […] ; and the way she laughed, cackling like a hen, the way she talked to the waiters and the maid, […]—all these unexpected phenomena impelled one to hysterical mirth, and made one class her with such immortally ludicrous types as Ally Sloper, the Widow Twankey, or Miss Moucher.

quote.citation: 1959, Georgette Heyer, chapter 1, in The Unknown Ajax:
quote.text: […] his lordship was out of humour. That was the way Chollacombe described as knaggy an old gager as ever Charles had had the ill-fortune to serve. Stiff-rumped, that's what he was, always rubbing the rust, or riding grub, like he had been for months past.

quote.text: An artificial kidney these days still means a refrigerator-sized dialysis machine. Such devices mimic the way real kidneys cleanse blood and eject impurities and surplus water as urine.

definitions.definition: A state or condition
Possibility (usually in the phrases 'any way' and 'no way').
Determined course; resolved mode of action or conduct.
(heading) Personal interaction.
(Germanic paganism) A tradition within the modern pagan faith of Heathenry, dedication to a specific deity or craft, Way of wyrd, Way of runes, Way of Thor etc.
(nautical, uncountable) Speed, progress, momentum.

quote.citation: 1855 December – 1857 June, Charles Dickens, Little Dorrit, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1857, →OCLC:
quote.text: Immediately afterwards, a quick and eager short dark man came into the room with so much way upon him that he was within a foot of Clennam before he could stop.

definitions.definition: A degree, an amount, a sense.

quote.text: That concertina was a wonder in its way. The handles that was on it first was wore out long ago, and he'd made new ones of braided rope yarn. And the bellows was patched in more places than a cranberry picker's overalls.

definitions.definition: (US, As the head of an interjectory clause, followed by an infinitive starting with “to”) Acknowledges that a task has been done well, chiefly in expressions of sarcastic congratulation.

definitions.definition: (plural only) The timbers of shipyard stocks that slope into the water and along which a ship or large boat is launched.

definitions.definition: (plural only) The longitudinal guiding surfaces on the bed of a planer, lathe, etc. along which a table or carriage moves.
(slang, only in reply to no way) yes; it is true; it is possible

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To travel.

definitions.definition: (informal, with an adverbial) Far.
